No hate to those who own 2x leveraged stocks, I have, and I'm sure most of us have, but this is why I don't recommend using them. 
This chart says it better than I can.
SanDisk is up 134% over six months. The 2x version is up 155%.
You took double the risk and got 1.15x the return.
But look at the peak. The leveraged fund was up over 800% while the stock was around 270%. It gave nearly all of it back. The stock held most of its gains. The leveraged version didn't.
That's volatility decay. A 2x fund gives you two times the daily return, not two times the return over time. Those are completely different things.
The math is simple. Stock up 10% then down 10% leaves you at 99%. The 2x version, up 20% then down 20%, leaves you at 96%. The stock lost 1%, you lost 4%. Nothing went wrong, the fund tracked perfectly, the rebalancing just ate you.
That compounds every single day the underlying chops, which is most days.
And it's worst on the most volatile names, which is exactly where these products exist.
They're built to be held for one day. The prospectus says so.
If you want leverage, use margin where you control the exposure, or just size up in the underlying.

So far this is the most interesting ones I have looked at.
$TMDX keeps donor organs alive during transport instead of packing them in ice. 
Their Organ Care System keeps a liver producing bile or a heart actually beating on the way to the operating room, which extends the viable window, lets surgeons assess function before implanting, and turns organs that would have been discarded into usable transplants.
The clinical evidence is what makes it work.
Their liver trial ran 300 patients across 20 US centers. Early allograft dysfunction dropped from 30.5% on ice to 17.3% on the machine. 
Ischemic biliary complications at twelve months fell from 9.9% to 2.6%. And utilization of organs from donation after cardiac death went from 24.5% to 45.9%, meaning nearly twice as many organs that would have been thrown away got used.
On the heart side, their expanded criteria trial took hearts that other centers had already refused an average of 65 times each, and transplanted 80% of them successfully.
Then there's the part that answers the obvious objection. Everyone asks why a hospital pays $38,000 to $80,000 for a machine when ice is free. 
The answer is that organ acquisition never got folded into the fixed Medicare payment system in 1983 the way everything else did. 
It's still reimbursed on a cost basis, and preservation is explicitly on the reimbursable list. The box isn't competing against free ice on the hospital's P&L. Also worth noting a heart transplant can total up to $2 million, so even the expensive version is a rounding error on the procedure.
Now the business.
Q2 revenue of $189.9 million, up 21%. Liver alone did $148 million, up 27.7%, and that segment has gone from $116 million to $148 million over the last four quarters. Gross margin at 60%, net income of $14.7 million, and $473 million in cash.
They also bought an aviation company in 2023 and now run 22 aircraft, 17 regional hubs, over 200 clinical staff, and a routing algorithm built with MIT. Roughly 99% of the business runs through their own logistics program, and service revenue is growing nearly twice as fast as product revenue.
A competitor can copy the box. Copying a private airline plus 200 clinical experts plus a decade of routing data is a different problem.
Management is targeting 10,000 US cases a year by 2028 and over $2 billion in revenue by 2032, against roughly $750 million this year.
So it's liver today, heart as a dated option, and kidney as the long term prize at three times liver's market size.
